title: The weekly and monthly review
teaches: Log every trade on the day, in R, with its setup and any rule you broke. Each week, turn the biggest leak into one concrete change and check last week's first. Each month, break every trade down by setup (count, win rate, average win and loss, average R), read it next to the market, and judge a setup only on a fair sample.

facts.quote: A good review is an efficient review, targeting our greatest successes and shortcomings on the day or week and then making those the focus on our efforts at improvement.
facts.claim: A good review picks out the biggest successes and the biggest shortcomings of the day or week, and makes those the focus.

facts.quote: Working on fewer goals more intensively leads to more lasting change. If we look at everything, we internalize very little.
facts.claim: A few goals worked on hard change more than a long list; look at everything and little sticks.

facts.quote: A review should finish with a highly concrete game plan for the next day, week, etc. A review without a plan is merely a look in the rear view mirror.
facts.claim: A review ends with a concrete plan for the next period, or it is only a look back.

facts.quote: "I traded too large, so I need to be more careful with my sizing tomorrow" might be a journal entry. That doesn't cut it. What, specifically will you do to be careful with your sizing?
facts.claim: A vague note like "be more careful with sizing" is not a plan; the plan says exactly what you will do.

facts.quote: They are throwaway - Once we conduct a review and set goals and plans, we need to then return to that review and those goals and plans after our next day or week of trading
facts.claim: A review you never come back to is a throwaway; after the next week, go back to its goals.

facts.quote: If not, we need to tweak our plans for the next time period. If we did succeed, we need to make note of what we did so that those actions can become more consistent
facts.claim: Missed the goal: adjust the plan. Hit it: write down what worked so you keep doing it.

facts.quote: If we don't revisit our goals and plans, we aren't truly holding ourselves accountable.
facts.claim: Goals you never check are goals nobody holds you to.

facts.quote: At the end of each month, I perform a post-analysis on all of my trades.
facts.claim: A money manager Steenbarger quotes reviews every one of his trades at the end of each month.

facts.quote: Sometimes breakouts are working, or mean reversion, or pullback trades. The only way to determine this is by breaking down every trade at the end of each month.
facts.claim: Which kind of setup is working changes, and a monthly breakdown of every trade shows which one it is.

facts.quote: Some quantitative examples are: % winners vs. losers; average win vs. loss; % of equity risked
facts.claim: The monthly numbers include the share of winners and the average win against the average loss.

facts.quote: That insight can also help him take more risk in favorable environments and pull back his risk taking in murky ones.
facts.claim: What the review shows can guide more risk when conditions suit you and less when they are murky.

facts.quote: The successful money managers I've worked with have had structured processes for previewing markets, viewing markets during trading hours, and reviewing trading once the day and week are finished.
facts.claim: The successful managers Steenbarger has worked with review their trading when each day and each week is done.

facts.quote: From this, I can set goals for the next month.
facts.claim: The monthly review sets the goals for the next month.

facts.quote: Invariably these reviews summarize what they did wrong over this period and how they could improve. They set lots of goals, but then that's often the last I hear about those goals until the next review period!
facts.claim: When a review sets lots of goals, Steenbarger often hears nothing more about them until the next review.

facts.quote: What if, at any given time, we worked on one goal and one goal only. Suppose we worked on it every single day and made it the focus on each day's efforts.
facts.claim: Steenbarger suggests working on one goal at a time, every day.

facts.quote: A trader may set a goal of trading with greater discipline, so that they stop overtrading.
facts.claim: "Trade with greater discipline" is Steenbarger's example of a goal a trader sets against overtrading.

facts.quote: A vague goal is only a good intention; it's not likely to energize or shape performance. My experience is that vague goals get the least follow-through.
facts.claim: A vague goal is only a good intention, and it gets the least follow-through.

facts.quote: Under what market conditions do I tend to make money? Lose money?
facts.claim: Measuring your results shows in which market conditions you make money and in which you lose it.

facts.quote: Which markets or types of trades tend to make and lose me money?
facts.claim: Measuring your results shows which types of trade make money and which lose it.

facts.quote: Still, the alternative to measurement is not intuition; it is ignorance.
facts.claim: Without measuring your results, what you have is not intuition but ignorance.

facts.quote: Our memories are biased by our emotions, as well as hindsight and the factors that most stick out in our mind.
facts.claim: Memory of a trade bends with emotion, hindsight and whatever stood out.

facts.quote: My general observation is that the frequency and intensity of review processes is associated with learning and performance improvement.
facts.claim: In Steenbarger's experience, reviewing more often and more deeply goes with learning and improving.

facts.quote: Review at the end of trading to assess whether rules were followed and especially to look at how a following of the rules could have improved the day's trading
facts.claim: The end-of-day review checks whether you followed your rules and what following them would have changed.

facts.quote: Targeting one or more rules to focus on for the coming session to improve trading.
facts.claim: The review picks the rule or rules to work on in the next session.

facts.quote: when we review only the things we do wrong--the result is a negative environment for our development.
facts.claim: Reviewing only what you did wrong makes a negative place to learn.

facts.quote: A best trading practice is using both successes and setbacks as fuel for learning and improvement.
facts.claim: Successes and setbacks are both material for learning.

facts.quote: The better trader makes active use of that journal to structure specific goals for the coming trading session/week and then holds themselves accountable for progress on those goals in their daily review.
facts.claim: The better trader sets specific goals for the coming week and checks progress on them every day.

facts.quote: They review their performance--good and bad--and they made dedicated efforts to learn from mistakes and best practices.
facts.claim: The best traders Steenbarger has worked with review both their good and their bad trading.

facts.quote: Eliminate setups not worth their intellectual, financial, and emotional capital
facts.claim: SMB's PlayBook Checkup, as Bellafiore and Spencer describe it, helps traders drop setups not worth their money and attention.

facts.quote: They are a way of focusing on process, rather than anchoring our moods and self-esteem to the ups and downs of P/L.
facts.claim: A journal keeps the focus on process instead of on the swings of P&L.

facts.quote: If you win a trade, then you want to know exactly why and how. More importantly, you want to know the same when you lose, so you don't repeat unnecessary mistakes.
facts.claim: Find out why and how on winners as well as losers, so you don't repeat mistakes.

facts.quote: After each trading day, adding up your profit or loss is secondary to knowing the why and how of your trading performance.
facts.claim: At the end of each day, knowing why and how you traded matters more than the P&L total.

facts.quote: Write down your daily conclusions in your trading journal so that you can reference them again later.
facts.claim: Write each day's conclusions down so you can come back to them later.

facts.quote: Constant assessment of your trading is one of the best ways to avoid repeating mistakes and to remind yourself of what has worked.
facts.claim: Assessing your trading all the time is one of the best ways to avoid repeat mistakes and remember what worked.

facts.quote: Be sure to save your trading records so you can go back and analyze elements such as: Profit or loss for a particular system or trading strategy
facts.claim: Keep your records so you can measure the profit or loss of each strategy.

facts.quote: Honesty and self-awareness are important traits for this exercise.
facts.claim: Reviewing your log takes honesty and self-awareness.

facts.quote: You should write a plan that has clear signals that aren't subject to change while you're trading, but they should be subject to reevaluation when the markets are closed.
facts.claim: The plan's signals are clear and fixed during the session, and you reevaluate them when the market is closed.

facts.quote: Refine your plan over time to adjust for changing market and economic circumstances.
facts.claim: A plan needs refining over time as markets change.

facts.quote: A frequent review and evaluation of trades is necessary to becoming a good trader.
facts.claim: Frequent review of your trades is part of becoming a good trader.

facts.quote: Evaluating and reviewing your past trades will allow you to identify patterns, strengths, and areas for improvement.
facts.claim: Reviewing past trades shows your patterns, your strengths and what to improve.

facts.quote: Losing streaks can happen to the best of us, but sometimes a bout of bad luck can actually reflect a problem with our trading strategy.
facts.claim: Losing streaks happen to good traders, though sometimes a streak does point to a real problem.

facts.quote: Attributing successes to our own skills but failures to uncontrollable outside forces is known as self-attribution bias.
facts.claim: Crediting wins to your skill and blaming losses on outside forces is self-attribution bias.

facts.quote: To begin, traders should look at whether they're losing or making money on a net basis, then look for patterns in their wins and losses.
facts.claim: After a losing streak, check whether you are up or down overall, then look for patterns in the wins and losses.

facts.quote: For example, if winning trades employ fundamental analysis and losing trades are based on technical analysis, a trader might want to focus more on fundamentals for a while.
facts.claim: If one kind of trade wins and another loses, lean toward the kind that wins for a while.

facts.quote: As a trader works to figure out what needs fixing, there's no harm in reducing the size of your trades.
facts.claim: While you work out what needs fixing, trading smaller is fine.

facts.quote: For example, if a long position starts losing money, traders may start buying more positions at lower prices or opening short positions on the same stock, thinking it's a way to get even with the market.
facts.claim: Buying more of a falling long to get even with the market is an emotional trading mistake.

facts.quote: There are many ways to avoid admitting you've made a mistake, but it's generally better to acknowledge a small loss than to keep digging in and lose more.
facts.claim: Better to take a small loss than to keep digging in and lose more.

facts.quote: Well, perhaps you didn't keep your word about taking a $1000 loss and failed to exit when you should have. Perhaps the market gapped down against you.
facts.claim: A loss bigger than planned can come from not taking the planned loss, or from a gap.

facts.quote: Losses bigger than 1R happen all the time. Your goal as a trader (or as an investor) is to keep your losses at 1R or less.
facts.claim: The goal is to keep every loss at 1R or less.

facts.quote: if you tend to blame someone else (your broker, your spouse, the person giving you tips) or even the market for the results that you get, then you will tend to repeat the same mistakes over and over again.
facts.claim: Blame others or the market for your results and you will tend to repeat the same mistakes.

facts.quote: If the total amount of money lost is greater than the total amount of money gained, you are a net loser and have a negative expectancy.
facts.claim: When the losses add up to more than the gains, the expectancy is negative.

facts.quote: it is much more efficient to think of the profits and losses of your trades as a ratio of the initial risk taken (R).
facts.claim: Think of every profit and loss as a multiple of the risk you took at entry, R.

facts.quote: Generally speaking, a sample needs more than thirty results before it can be considered having any statistical significance.
facts.claim: As a rough rule, a sample needs more than thirty results before it means much.

facts.quote: Expectancy is best stated in terms of how much you can make per dollar you risk. Expectancy is the mean R of an R-multiple distribution generated by a trading system.
facts.claim: Expectancy is the average R per trade: what a system makes per dollar risked.

facts.quote: The percentage of closed trades in which you make money.
facts.claim: Win rate is the share of closed trades that make money.

facts.quote: Trading system performance varies by market type allowing traders to develop optimally performing trading systems for each type or to vary position sizing strategies by type.
facts.claim: A system's results vary with the kind of market, so traders can size differently in each kind.

facts.quote: When a sample size is too small, accurate and trustworthy conclusions cannot be drawn.
facts.claim: Too small a sample gives no trustworthy conclusion.

facts.quote: Even with a high win rate, a poor risk/reward ratio can lead to losses.
facts.claim: A high win rate can still lose money when the losses are big next to the wins.

facts.quote: You've also stopped journaling when your performance has been so bad you don't want to review it and make yourself feel worse.
facts.claim: Tendler's readers have stopped journaling when results were so bad they didn't want to review them.

facts.quote: Is there a common mistake that is cropping up time and again that you need to focus on to avoid this in the future?
facts.claim: The review looks for the mistake that keeps cropping up, so you can focus on it.

facts.quote: I know you don't want to. You want to move on and not focus on it anymore. But you can't.
facts.claim: After a bad session you won't want to journal about it, and Tendler says do it anyway.

facts.quote: Note that Ryan is reviewing both the market environment and his specific trades.
facts.claim: The money manager's monthly review covers the market environment as well as his own trades.

facts.quote: In order to really get a clear picture of the system's expectancy, you should actually have somewhere between 100 and 200.
facts.claim: A clear picture of a system's expectancy takes somewhere between 100 and 200 trades.

facts.quote: Ideally this should be done away from the excitement and gyrations of the market, so weekends can be a good idea.
facts.claim: Review away from the live market; the weekend is a good time.

walkthroughs.title: Three clocks
steps: Every day, log each trade while it's fresh: the setup, the result in R, and any rule you broke.
Every week, check last week's change first. Then pick the biggest leak and turn it into one concrete change.
Every month, sort every trade by setup and see what the market is paying for. That sets next month's goals.

walkthroughs.title: A setup's numbers
steps: For each setup, count the trades, the win rate, and the average win and loss.
Add the results in R and divide by the count. That average R is what the setup has paid per trade.
Few trades, little proof. Tharp wants over thirty results for a rough read, and 100 to 200 for a clear one.

walkthroughs.title: The mistake audit
steps: Go back through your recent trades and tag every rule you broke.
Add up what each kind of mistake cost you in R.
The costliest one becomes next week's single goal. Write exactly what you'll do differently.
Next Sunday, check that goal before you set anything new.

questions.q: Once you have a good trading plan, you can stop reviewing your trades.
questions.why: False. Frequent review is part of becoming a good trader, and a plan needs refining as markets change. The review is where that refining happens.
questions.lesson_line: A plan is where you start. The review keeps it current.

questions.q: A good review looks only at your losing trades.
questions.why: False. You want to know why a winner worked as well as why a loser failed. Steenbarger warns that reviewing only what you did wrong makes a negative place to learn.
questions.lesson_line: Study your best trades as hard as your worst. The winners show you what to repeat.

questions.q: Trade A risked $200 and made $500. Trade B risked $1,000 and made $1,500. Which did better for its risk?
choices: Trade A, at 2.5R
Trade B, it made $1,000 more
Neither, the sizes differ too much
questions.why: Trade A, at 2.5R. $500 on $200 of risk is 2.5R. Trade B made only one and a half times its risk. In R, trades of every size line up.
questions.lesson_line: Log every result in R. Then a small trade and a big one compare fairly.

wrong.Trade B, it made $1,000 more: More dollars, but it risked five times as much to get them. For the risk taken, B did worse.
wrong.Neither, the sizes differ too much: That's exactly what R fixes. Dividing by the risk puts both trades on the same scale.

questions.q: Fill in the word.
questions.sentence: Each month, sort every trade by ___ to see which kinds of trade are paying.
questions.why: Setup. A money manager Steenbarger quotes breaks down every trade each month to see whether breakouts, pullbacks or something else is working.
questions.lesson_line: One pile per setup. The piles show where your money really comes from.

wrong.share price: A stock's price doesn't tell you what kind of trade it was.
wrong.broker: Your broker fills the orders. It doesn't change which setups work.
wrong.account: Sorting by account mixes every kind of trade back together.

questions.q: Your monthly review should look at what the market did, not just at your trades.
questions.why: True. Results change with conditions. The money manager Steenbarger quotes reviews the market environment as well as his trades, and Tharp notes a system's performance varies by market type.
questions.lesson_line: Read your stats next to the market they came from.

questions.q: Which numbers belong in each setup's monthly stats?
choices: Count, win rate, average win and loss
Win rate and number of trades only
The setup's total dollar P&L
questions.answer: Count, win rate, average win and loss
questions.why: Count, win rate, average win and loss. Together they give you the average R the setup has paid. A high win rate can still lose money if the losses are big next to the wins.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate is half the story. How big the wins and losses run is the other half.

wrong.Win rate and number of trades only: That leaves out how big the wins and losses are. Even with a high win rate, a poor risk/reward can lose.
wrong.The setup's total dollar P&L: One total hides the parts. It can't show how often the setup wins or how big its wins and losses run.

questions.q: Your gut sense of which setups work is as reliable as your trade stats.
questions.why: False. Memory bends with emotion and hindsight, and gut feel runs on memory. The alternative to measuring, Steenbarger says, is not intuition but ignorance.
questions.lesson_line: Trust the ledger over the feeling. The feeling remembers the trades that stood out. The ledger remembers all of them.

questions.q: Your review shows you overtrade. Which note is a plan you can act on next week?
choices: Stop after three trades each day
Be more careful with my trading plan
Trade with more discipline
Make fewer mistakes next week
questions.answer: Stop after three trades each day
questions.why: Stop after three trades each day. It's concrete, and next Sunday you can check whether you kept it. A vague goal, Steenbarger says, is only a good intention.
questions.lesson_line: If you can't check it next week, it isn't a plan.

wrong.Be more careful with my trading plan: Careful how. Steenbarger's test is what, specifically, you will do. This note doesn't say.
wrong.Trade with more discipline: That's Steenbarger's own example of a vague goal against overtrading. It names a wish, not an action.
wrong.Make fewer mistakes next week: Which ones, and how. Vague goals get the least follow-through.

questions.q: Ten breakout trades, in R: +2, -1, -1, +3, -1.5, +2.5, -1, -0.5, +2.5, -1. What's the win rate?
questions.why: 40%. Four of the ten trades made money. Win rate is the share of closed trades that make money.
questions.lesson_line: Count the winners and divide by all the trades. Then check how big they were.

questions.q: Same ten trades: +2, -1, -1, +3, -1.5, +2.5, -1, -0.5, +2.5, -1. What's the average R per trade?
questions.why: +0.4R a trade. Add the ten results and divide by ten. It's positive even though six of the ten lost. Ten trades is a first read, not proof.
questions.lesson_line: Average R, not win rate, tells you what a setup has paid. A 40% win rate can still earn.

questions.story: Sunday review. Your list of things to fix has eight items. Chasing entries keep showing up, and they cost you the most R by far.
questions.q: What goes into next week's plan?
choices: One fix, for the chasing
All eight, so nothing gets missed
Nothing yet, review again next week
questions.why: One fix, for the chasing. Target the mistake that keeps cropping up and costs the most. As Steenbarger puts it, look at everything and you take in very little.
questions.lesson_line: One leak at a time. Plug the biggest one first.

wrong.All eight, so nothing gets missed: Long goal lists fade. Steenbarger often hears nothing more about them until the next review.
wrong.Nothing yet, review again next week: A review without a plan is only a look in the rear view mirror. Meanwhile the chasing keeps costing you.

questions.story: Last Sunday you set one goal: no new trades in the first 15 minutes. Now it's Sunday again.
questions.q: What does your review do first?
choices: Check if you kept last week's goal
Set three new goals for this week
Add up the week's P&L
questions.answer: Check if you kept last week's goal
questions.why: Check if you kept last week's goal. Steenbarger calls a review you never come back to a throwaway. If you kept it, note what worked. If not, tweak the plan.
questions.lesson_line: Every review opens with last week's goal. A goal nobody checks was only a wish.

wrong.Set three new goals for this week: New goals on top of an unchecked one is how goals pile up and fade. Check the old one first.
wrong.Add up the week's P&L: The P&L is the score. Whether you kept your goal is the part you control.

questions.q: Your last 20 trades: 6 broke a rule and lost 7R in total. The other 14 made +9R. What did all 20 make, in R?
questions.why: +2R. The rule breaks gave back 7R of the 9R the clean trades made. Pricing your mistakes in R shows you what they really cost.
questions.lesson_line: Add up your mistakes in R. The costliest one is next week's fix.

questions.q: Your last ten losses, sized in R: 1, 1, 1.2, 0.8, 1, 2.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.5. How big is the average loss?
questions.why: 1.2R. Add the ten losses and divide by ten. A planned loss is 1R, so some losses ran past the stop. Tharp's goal is losses at 1R or less.
questions.lesson_line: An average loss above 1R is a leak. Find the trades that ran past the stop.

questions.story: You added a new pullback setup this month. Four trades, four losses, each about 1R. You followed your rules every time.
questions.q: What does the monthly review say about it?
choices: Too few trades to judge it yet
It's broken, drop it now
Double the size to win it back
questions.answer: Too few trades to judge it yet
questions.why: Too few trades to judge it yet. Four results say very little, and Tharp's rough bar is more than thirty. Keep logging it, smaller if you like, while the sample grows.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a setup on a sample, not a streak.

wrong.It's broken, drop it now: That's a verdict from four results. Losing streaks happen to good setups too.
wrong.Double the size to win it back: That raises your risk exactly when you know least. Schwab's advice runs the other way: trade smaller while you work out what's wrong.

questions.q: A string of losses means your strategy has stopped working.
questions.why: False. Losing streaks happen to good strategies too, though sometimes a streak does point to a real problem. Look for patterns in the wins and losses before you decide.
questions.lesson_line: A streak is a question, not an answer. Your ledger answers it.

questions.story: Your weekly review says the three winners were great reads. The five losers were bad luck, a rigged market and surprise news.
questions.q: What's wrong with this review?
choices: Wins get credit, losses get excuses
Nothing, losses are often bad luck
It has too many losing trades
questions.answer: Wins get credit, losses get excuses
questions.why: Wins get credit, losses get excuses. Schwab calls that self-attribution bias. Tharp's warning: blame the market for your results and you'll tend to repeat the same mistakes.
questions.lesson_line: Own the losers as fully as the winners. That's where the lessons hide.

wrong.Nothing, losses are often bad luck: Some losses are bad luck. All five being bad luck, while every win was skill, is the bias talking.
wrong.It has too many losing trades: The count isn't the problem. Blaming every one of the losers on outside forces is.

questions.story: Your plan caps every loss at 1R. One line in your ledger reads -3R. There was no gap that day. You bought more twice as it fell.
questions.q: How does the review file that loss?
choices: A rule break: adding to a loser
Bad luck: it just kept falling
A setup problem: drop the setup
questions.answer: A rule break: adding to a loser
questions.why: A rule break: adding to a loser. Tharp names two ways a loss runs past 1R: a gap, or not taking the loss you planned. There was no gap, and the adds made it bigger.
questions.lesson_line: A loss bigger than 1R is a flag. Find the rule that bent.

wrong.Bad luck: it just kept falling: Falling past your planned exit was the stop's job to handle. Buying more on the way down made the loss bigger, by choice.
wrong.A setup problem: drop the setup: The setup's risk was 1R. The extra loss came from the adds, not from the entry.

questions.q: 'Make $2,000 next week' is a good goal to take from your weekly review.
questions.why: False. You can't order the market to pay you a set amount. A goal from the review names something you will do, like an entry rule you'll keep, and next Sunday you check it.
questions.lesson_line: Set goals for how you trade. The money is the result, not the plan.

questions.story: Your breakouts paid for months. This month the market chopped sideways, and they lost on 9 of 11 tries, all taken by your rules.
questions.q: What does the review do with breakouts?
choices: Cut breakout size for now
Keep full size, they'll come back
Drop breakouts for good
questions.why: Cut breakout size for now. Tharp notes results vary with the kind of market, and the money manager Steenbarger quotes takes less risk when conditions are murky. Schwab adds there's no harm in trading smaller while you work it out.
questions.lesson_line: Size follows the market. Less when it fights your setup, more when it pays it.

wrong.Keep full size, they'll come back: Maybe they will, but nothing promises it. Results vary with the kind of market, and this one isn't paying breakouts.
wrong.Drop breakouts for good: Eleven tries in one kind of market isn't the whole record. Months of results say the setup works when the market suits it.

questions.story: Your earnings-gap setup: 45 trades over five months, all by your rules. It averaged -0.3R a trade.
questions.q: What does the review say?
choices: Bench it and work out why
Too few trades to judge yet
Size up to win the losses back
questions.answer: Bench it and work out why
questions.why: Bench it and work out why. Forty-five trades clears Tharp's rough bar of more than thirty results, and the negative average R says it has lost money so far. Stop paying for it until you know why.
questions.lesson_line: A setup that loses over a fair sample, traded right, gets benched. Not sized up.

wrong.Too few trades to judge yet: Forty-five is past Tharp's rough bar of thirty. Not proof, but enough to stop paying for it while you find out why.
wrong.Size up to win the losses back: Expectancy is what you make per dollar risked. More dollars on a negative average just lose more.

questions.story: Worst week of the year. Down on almost every trade. The last thing you want on Sunday is to open the journal.
questions.q: What do you do with the weekly review?
choices: Run it as usual
Skip it and start fresh Monday
Review only the winners this week
questions.why: Run it as usual. Bad stretches are exactly when people stop reviewing, as Tendler notes. Look for the patterns in the losses. That's how you find what to fix.
questions.lesson_line: The week you least want to review is the one you most need to.

wrong.Skip it and start fresh Monday: Then Monday starts with whatever caused the losses still in place.
wrong.Review only the winners this week: This week the losses hold the lesson. You want to know why you lost, so you don't repeat it.

questions.story: Your last 20 trades. Breakouts: 9 trades, +6R. Gap plays: 4 trades, +1R. Pullbacks: 7 trades, -5R, where 5 chased entries lost 6R and 2 clean ones made 1R.
questions.q: What do you fix first?
choices: The chasing on pullbacks
Drop pullbacks for good
Drop gap plays, too few trades
Trade only breakouts from now on
questions.why: The chasing on pullbacks. The five chased entries lost 6R, and the two taken by your rules made 1R. The leak is the chasing, and seven trades can't judge a setup anyway.
questions.lesson_line: Fix the behavior before you blame the setup.

wrong.Drop pullbacks for good: The chased entries made the losses. You'd be firing the setup for your own mistake.
wrong.Drop gap plays, too few trades: Too few trades is a reason to keep logging, not to drop. Four results say little either way.
wrong.Trade only breakouts from now on: Nine trades don't prove breakouts either. And the biggest leak in this ledger is a behavior, not a setup.

questions.story: Both setups traded by your rules. Setup A: 40 trades, won 70%, averaged -0.1R. Setup B: 40 trades, won 35%, averaged +0.4R.
questions.q: Which one gets more of your size next month?
choices: Setup B, it pays more per trade
Setup A, it wins twice as often
Neither, both samples are too small
questions.answer: Setup B, it pays more per trade
questions.why: Setup B, it pays more per trade. Expectancy is the average R, and B's is positive while A's is negative. A high win rate can still lose when the losses outweigh the wins.
questions.lesson_line: Size goes where the average R is, not where the win rate is.

wrong.Setup A, it wins twice as often: Winning often isn't the goal. A loses a little on average every trade, however often it wins.
wrong.Neither, both samples are too small: Both clear Tharp's rough bar of more than thirty results. That's a fair first read, not proof, and the gap between them is wide.

conflicts: Sample size: Tharp's glossary says a sample needs 'more than thirty results' for any significance (f53); his concepts page says 'a minimum of thirty trades' for a good idea of expectancy and 'somewhere between 100 and 200' for a clear picture (f64, added by the checker). The file uses 'more than thirty' only as a rough first bar (w2, q15, q21, q24), never as proof: w2 now names the 100 to 200, q21's key is 'bench it and work out why' (not 'drop it'), and q21/q24's notes say 'not proof'.

Cadence: the unit row says 'weekly setup stats'. A swing trader's week holds only a few trades per setup, which the sample-size facts (f53, f57) say cannot support a conclusion, so this file puts setup stats in the monthly (or longer) review, as the money manager quoted in s2 does (f08, f09), and keeps the weekly review for the one biggest leak and last week's goal (f01, f05). Owner's call if he wants weekly stats.

The monthly post-analysis (f08, f09, f10, f13) is money manager Ryan Worch's practice, quoted on Steenbarger's blog, not Steenbarger's own rule; the questions say 'a money manager Steenbarger quotes'. f11 is Steenbarger's own comment on it.
CME's trade-log page lists 'Drawdowns (maximum loss per trade using a trading system)', which is not the usual meaning of drawdown (peak-to-trough fall in the account). Not used.

Steenbarger's single-goal advice (f02, f15) is his coaching view; CME (f34) and Investopedia (f40) agree the review is for finding and fixing mistakes but do not say 'one at a time'. Checker: CME was q11's only second publisher and does not back focusing on one mistake, so f61 (CMC Markets: the 'common mistake that is cropping up time and again that you need to focus on') was added, the story now says the chasing keeps showing up, and the key was softened from 'nothing else' to 'One fix, for the chasing'. Steenbarger stays credited by name for 'look at everything'.
Steenbarger (2026-10 entries) also lists reviewing the trades you missed as a best practice; no second publisher in this pass says it, so it is not asked.
